extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, and writers interested in the science fiction genre
extracted.subtask_description: Overview of conventions, definitions, subgenre distinctions, themes, and evaluative perspectives useful for creating or assessing science fiction works. Summarizes what critics and practitioners consider characteristic or valuable in SF.

rubrics_metrics.name: Core definition: speculation about science and technology
rubrics_metrics.description: Science fiction is the genre of speculative fiction that imagines advanced and futuristic scientific or technological progress and often explores human responses to the consequences of these types of projected or imagined scientific advances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple quoted definitions appear: Isaac Asimov — "that branch of literature which deals with the reaction of human beings to changes in science and technology"; Robert A. Heinlein — "realistic speculation about possible future events, based solidly on adequate knowledge of the real world, past and present, and on a thorough understanding of the nature and significance of the scientific method." Use of these definitions implies works should (a) imagine plausible scientific/technological change and (b) foreground human reactions or consequences. The article notes no single universally satisfactory definition and that enthusiasts often act as arbiters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technological impossibility / extrapolation criterion (DK/Gernsback)
rubrics_metrics.description: Science fiction includes "scenarios that are at the time of writing technologically impossible, extrapolating from present-day science... or that deal with some form of speculative science-based conceit."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gernsback's early notion ('scientifiction') emphasized mixing scientific fact with prophetic vision and instructiveness: stories should be plausibly extrapolated from known science and can supply knowledge. For writers/evaluators: consider whether the conceit extrapolates logically from current science and whether the story handles that extrapolation in a way that feels coherent and informative rather than gratuitous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typical elements and themes
rubrics_metrics.description: Elements common to science fiction include space exploration, extraterrestrial life, time travel, robotics, parallel universes, dystopian societies, biological manipulations, information technology, transhumanism, posthumanism, and environmental challenges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The presence of one or more of these elements is characteristic but not mandatory. Use the list to identify genre expectations, thematic focus, and potential tropes; mixing or subverting these elements is common. Evaluators can check how central these elements are to the story's speculative premise and whether they are handled thoughtfully rather than as mere decoration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hard vs soft science fiction (feasibility emphasis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hard science fiction emphasizes scientific accuracy; soft science fiction focuses on the social sciences. The historical distinction centers on the feasibility of the science used in the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definitions and commentary: hard SF often foregrounds physics/astronomy/mathematics/engineering and strives for technical rigor (Max Gladstone: 'where the math works'); soft SF draws on biology, sociology, anthropology and prioritizes social/character issues (Ursula K. Le Guin's critique of hard/soft boundaries). For writers: choose the emphasis (technical rigor vs social plausibility) and maintain consistent internal standards. For evaluators: judge fidelity to declared emphasis — e.g., hard SF should support its science plausibly; soft SF should convincingly engage social/psychological aspects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subgenre emphasis as evaluative criterion (space opera, cyberpunk, cli‑fi, etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Subgenres define particular emphases: space opera 'emphasizes pure adventure' in a universe with common space travel; cyberpunk 'explores the interface between technology and society'; climate fiction addresses environmental issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When producing or assessing a work within a named subgenre, check whether it embodies the subgenre's hallmark concerns and tone (e.g., adventure and grand scale for space opera; near-future tech and social decay for cyberpunk; ecological stakes for cli‑fi). Subgenre expectations guide setting, stakes, and thematic focus; successful works may also subvert or hybridize subgenre conventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sense of wonder
rubrics_metrics.description: Science fiction's appeal often lies in an ability to inspire a 'sense of wonder' by combining the rational and believable with the miraculous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: David Hartwell: 'Science fiction's appeal lies in [the] combination of the rational, the believable, with the miraculous.' Carl Sagan's reflections echo SF's role in conveying awe and curiosity. For writers: cultivate moments that evoke awe without sacrificing internal coherence. For evaluators: consider whether the work evokes wonder in a way that feels earned by the speculative premise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of science fiction as social critique / protest literature
rubrics_metrics.description: Science fiction can criticize present-day society and explore alternatives; it has been used as protest literature (e.g., Orwell's Nineteen Eighty-Four).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: SF often refracts contemporary social, political, and ethical issues through speculative settings. Assess whether the critique is integrated into the narrative (show, don't preach), whether alternatives are imaginatively developed, and whether the work illuminates present concerns via extrapolation rather than simple allegory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character-centered literary merit
rubrics_metrics.description: Serious literary value in science fiction is often tied to treatment of character; Ursula K. Le Guin: 'all novels ... deal with character... Otherwise, they would not be novelists.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arguments in the article note skepticism about genre fiction's literary value but emphasize that strong characterization differentiates 'serious' fiction. For writers: develop characters deeply even when plotting speculative ideas. For evaluators: weigh character depth, development, and ability to carry themes alongside speculative concepts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimentation and New Wave sensibility
rubrics_metrics.description: New Wave science fiction embraced a high degree of experimentation (in both form and content) and a self-consciously 'literary' or 'artistic' sensibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This criterion values formal innovation, stylistic risk, and thematic complexity. For writers: experimentation should serve thematic or emotional aims rather than be novelty for its own sake. For evaluators: consider whether formal experiments enhance understanding or resonance, and whether they are coherent within the work's aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem‑solving ethos (practical method in hard SF)
rubrics_metrics.description: An alternative way to define hard SF is by characters striving to solve problems 'in the right way — with determination, a touch of stoicism, and the consciousness that the universe is not on his or her side.' (Michael Swanwick)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This emphasizes methodical, engineering-minded approaches to plot conflicts. Writers of problem-driven SF should show plausible methods and the intellectual work of problem solving; evaluators can judge whether problem-solving sequences are credible, logically structured, and integrated with character and theme.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification by focus of science (natural vs social sciences)
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories focusing explicitly on physics/astronomy/mathematics/engineering tend to be classed as hard SF, while those focusing on botany/mycology/zoology and the social sciences tend to be classed as soft SF.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this as a heuristic for categorization and expectations: the disciplinary focus shapes plausibility claims, research needs for the writer, and aesthetic priorities. When assessing, ask whether the work's scientific focus is treated with appropriate depth and whether it supports the story's stakes.
